sections.content:
You know *debido a* and *a raíz de* from B1 Unit 6: both give a cause and take a noun. Formal Spanish has other phrases like them, and each says what *kind* of cause it is. This lesson sorts three:

• *a raíz de*: an event that set something off. What follows is a reaction ("following", "as a result of").
• *con motivo de*: the occasion for something, usually a special event such as an anniversary or a visit ("on the occasion of", "to mark").
• *en virtud de*: the rule, right or power that allows or requires an act ("by virtue of", "under").

All three are followed by a noun, never by a conjugated verb, and they usually open the sentence, followed by a comma. Remember that *de* + *el* becomes *del*: *a raíz del accidente*.

sections.title: Three kinds of cause
rows: A raíz del accidente, la ciudad cambió las normas de tráfico.
Following the accident, the city changed its traffic rules.
Con motivo del aniversario, el museo abrió gratis todo el fin de semana.
To mark its anniversary, the museum opened free all weekend.
En virtud de la ley, los empleados tienen derecho a vacaciones pagadas.
Under the law, employees are entitled to paid holidays.

sections.content: Ask what kind of cause you mean: an event that came first (*a raíz de*), a special occasion (*con motivo de*), or a rule or authority (*en virtud de*). If the cause is a whole clause with a verb, use *porque* instead: *porque llovía*, but *a raíz de la lluvia*.
